newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore January exports on slow path to recovery.
newsitem.headline: Singapore January exports on slow path to recovery.

text.p: Singapore's non-oil exports were still showing signs of weakness in January but seemed to be on track for a gradual recovery by the middle of the year, economists said on Wednesday.
A Reuter poll of 17 financial institutions this week showed an average forecast of a 1.0 percent fall year-on-year in nominal terms for non-oil exports in January.
The institutions said, however, that Singapore's exports on a monthly basis showed a small but positive bias.
They attributed the expected January fall to a comparatively high base in January 1996.
"The year-on-year comparison was against a very high base, right around the peak when people read the electronics sector wrong," said Tan Min Lan, economist with Merrill Lynch.
January 1996 non-oil exports were a robust 24 percent higher that in the previous January, but this was followed by fall of 5.2 percent in February and an 8.5 percent drop in March.

In the first quarter last year, Asian producers of electronic and computer components rushed to increase output in anticipation of higher world demand. A downturn in the second half of the year left stocks on their hands, the economists said "Looking at leading indicators on global orders, exports here should improve in about four to six months," Prasenjit Basu, economist with UBS Securities said.
He echoed the general view that the pace of recovery was making headway but would not be evident until mid-year and export data could still show year-on-year declines.
Others said they preferred to combine January with February estimates, to reduce the probability of distortion during the festive New Year and Lunar New Year periods which fell in February.
Singapore's general election on January 2 was also seen dampening exports as businesses shut for a public holiday.

"The margin of error could be quite large now....(but) the big computer companies are under-producing in terms of demand and we should see some catching up, possibly in April," Liew Yin Sze, economist with J.M. Sassoon said.

The same Reuters poll produced an average forecast of a rise of 2.0 percent year-on-year in January for Singapore's consumer price index (CPI) of inflation. This compares to a CPI reading of 1.4 percent for the entire year of 1996.
Economists called this a stable level for January, with high food prices during the festive period causing the most pressure.
The costs of other items were seen flat with consumer spending somewhat restrained by a bearish economic outlook.
Singapore's export figures wwere dur to be published on Thursday, and CPI data on Sunday.
